The middlewares will be applied in the order they are provided.  ```ts const wrappedLanguageModel = wrapLanguageModel({   model: yourModel,   middleware: [firstMiddleware, secondMiddleware], });  // applied as: firstMiddleware(secondMiddleware(yourModel)) ```  ## Built-in Middleware  The AI SDK comes with several built-in middlewares that you can use to configure language models:  - `extractReasoningMiddleware`: Extracts reasoning information from the generated text and exposes it as a `reasoning` property on the result. - `simulateStreamingMiddleware`: Simulates streaming behavior with responses from non-streaming language models. - `defaultSettingsMiddleware`: Applies default settings to a language model.  ### Extract Reasoning  Some providers and models expose reasoning information in the generated text using special tags, e.g. \ and \.  The `extractReasoningMiddleware` function can be used to extract this reasoning information and expose it as a `reasoning` property on the result.  ```ts import { wrapLanguageModel, extractReasoningMiddleware } from 'ai';  const model = wrapLanguageModel({   model: yourModel,   middleware: extractReasoningMiddleware({ tagName: 'think' }), }); ```  You can then use that enhanced model in functions like `generateText` and `streamText`.  The `extractReasoningMiddleware` function also includes a `startWithReasoning` option. When set to `true`, the reasoning tag will be prepended to the generated text. This is useful for models that do not include the reasoning tag at the beginning of the response. For more details, see the [DeepSeek R1 guide](/v5/docs/guides/r1#deepseek-r1-middleware).  ### Simulate Streaming  The `simulateStreamingMiddleware` function can be used to simulate streaming behavior with responses from non-streaming language models. This is useful when you want to maintain a consistent streaming interface even when using models that only provide complete responses.  ```ts import { wrapLanguageModel, simulateStreamingMiddleware } from 'ai';  const model = wrapLanguageModel({   model: yourModel,   middleware: simulateStreamingMiddleware(), }); ```  ### Default Settings  The `defaultSettingsMiddleware` function can be used to apply default settings to a language model.  ```ts import { wrapLanguageModel, defaultSettingsMiddleware } from 'ai';  const model = wrapLanguageModel({   model: yourModel,   middleware: defaultSettingsMiddleware({     settings: {       temperature: 0.5,       maxOutputTokens: 800,       providerOptions: { openai: { store: false } },     },   }), }); ```  ## Community Middleware  The AI SDK provides a Language Model Middleware specification. Community members can develop middleware that adheres to this specification, making it compatible with the AI SDK ecosystem.  Here are some community middlewares that you can explore:  ### Custom tool call parser  The [Custom tool call parser](https://github.com/minpeter/ai-sdk-tool-call-middleware) middleware extends tool call capabilities to models that don't natively support the OpenAI-style `tools` parameter. This includes many self-hosted and third-party models that lack native function calling features.  Using this middleware on models that support native function calls may result in unintended performance degradation, so check whether your model supports native function calls before deciding to use it.  This middleware enables function calling capabilities by converting function schemas into prompt instructions and parsing the model's responses into structured function calls. It works by transforming the JSON function definitions into natural language instructions the model can understand, then analyzing the generated text to extract function call attempts. This approach allows developers to use the same function calling API across different model providers, even with models that don't natively support the OpenAI-style function calling format, providing a consistent function calling experience regardless of the underlying model implementation.  The `@ai-sdk-tool/parser` package offers three middleware variants:  - `createToolMiddleware`: A flexible function for creating custom tool call middleware tailored to specific models - `hermesToolMiddleware`: Ready-to-use middleware for Hermes & Qwen format function calls - `gemmaToolMiddleware`: Pre-configured middleware for Gemma 3 model series function call format  Here's how you can enable function calls with Gemma models that don't support them natively:  ```ts import { wrapLanguageModel } from 'ai'; import { gemmaToolMiddleware } from '@ai-sdk-tool/parser';  const model = wrapLanguageModel({   model: openrouter('google/gemma-3-27b-it'),   middleware: gemmaToolMiddleware, }); ```  Find more examples at this [link](https://github.com/minpeter/ai-sdk-tool-call-middleware/tree/main/examples/core/src).  ## Implementing Language Model Middleware  Implementing language model middleware is advanced functionality and requires a solid understanding of the [language model specification](https://github.com/vercel/ai/blob/release-v5.0/packages/provider/src/language-model/v2/language-model-v2.ts). # Report Land results

Default to ordinary prose with no `<land-result>` block.

Emit a block only when reporting the final outcome of a landing skill the
user invoked. Work that prepares for a later landing is not that invocation,
even when the requested task is complete. Loading this reporting skill does
not satisfy the condition either. In those cases, do not emit a
`<land-result>` tag for any outcome.

- **Success (`landed`):** The requested change has reached the workflow's
  final remote destination, and you verified it there.
- **Failure (`failed`):** An actual failure or blocker prevents landing, and
  you cannot proceed with permitted safe recovery. Explain what failed or
  blocked the operation and any action needed from the user.
- **Neither:** The operation is being set up, is in progress, or is waiting
  for CI, review, approval, or routine user input. Completed preparatory work
  is still neither while landing remains outstanding. Continuing retries and
  no-ops where the change was already present are also neither. Describe these
  states in ordinary prose without a structured result.

Ending a turn does not make the Land operation successful or failed. For
success or failure, include exactly one structured result in the final
response. Nothing follows it except the first-use alert described below.

For a verified landing:

```text
<land-result outcome="landed" target="main" target-url="https://github.com/org/repo/tree/main" commit="abc1234" commit-url="https://github.com/org/repo/commit/abc1234" ci-status="passed" ci-url="https://github.com/org/repo/actions/runs/123" />
```

For a blocking failure:

```text
<land-result outcome="failed" target="main" ci-status="failed" ci-url="https://github.com/org/repo/actions/runs/123">
CI failed after the final retry because the Linux integration test timed out.
</land-result>
```

The attributes have a fixed meaning:

- `outcome` is required and must be `landed` or `failed`.
- `target` names the destination branch. `target-url` links to it.
- `commit` is the short landed or attempted commit identifier. `commit-url` links to it.
- `ci-status` is `passed` or `failed`. `ci-url` links to the run.

Include optional attributes only when you know their values. Never invent a

# Technical writing

The goal is writing a tired engineer understands on the first read. Four layers get you there, one question each: what kind of document is this, how do sentences address the reader, how much does each sentence carry, and can any sentence be read two ways. Apply all four.

Three rules sit above the layers:

- **Cut every word that does no work.** If the sentence survives without a word, the word goes. "In order to" is "to". "It is important to note that" is nothing.
- **Use the short, everyday word.** "Use", not "utilize". "Help", not "facilitate". "Do", not "perform". A long word has to buy its length with precision.
- **When a rule makes a sentence worse, fix the sentence another way or leave it alone.** The rules serve the reader. A sentence that follows every rule and sounds like a machine wrote it has failed.

The codebase is the word list. Write the real symbol, file, flag, or command name, not a synonym or a description of it.

Don't invent jargon. Use the words a developer would say out loud: "move", "delete", "a budget that only decreases", not "evacuate", "ratchet", or "endgame". A named pattern is fine when the doc says what it means the first time. Add new offenders and their replacements to rule 26 in `references/unslop.md`.

## Vary the rhythm

The layers decide what a document says and how much each sentence carries. A doc can obey all of them and still read machine-written: every sentence clipped short, no view anywhere, nothing specific.

- Mix sentence lengths on purpose. Short sentences land a point. Longer ones that take their time carry a fact with its condition or consequence.
- One thought per sentence does not mean one length per sentence. Split the sentence that carries two thoughts. Keep the long sentence that carries one.
- Have a view where the mode allows it. Explanation weighs trade-offs, so say what you make of them instead of listing pros and cons. Reference stays dry.
- Be specific over sterile. Not "schema changes can cause issues" but "a column rename fails the build".

## Pick the mode first (Diátaxis)

One document, one mode. For a ground-up tutorial, study guide, or cheat sheet that teaches a domain from its smallest unit, use the textbook mode in `references/textbook.md` instead. Two questions pick the Diátaxis mode: does the content inform action (doing) or understanding (thinking), and does it serve learning or work?

- Action + learning: **tutorial**.
- Action + work: **how-to**.
- Understanding + work: **reference**.
- Understanding + learning: **explanation**.

Use the compass on a whole document or on one sentence. Reach for it whenever you feel unsure what you are writing. Gut feel is often wrong here.

**Tutorial: learning by doing.** You are the teacher. The learner's success is your job, not theirs. Open by saying what the learner will build, not what they will "learn". Every step produces a visible result, early and often. Tell them what they should see: the expected output, the prompt change, the log line. Cut explanation to one clause and a link. Teaching pauses break the lesson. Stay concrete. Write as "we", in commands: "First, do x. Now, do y."

**How-to: steps to a goal.** Solve a problem a person has, not an operation the machine can perform. Assume competence. Skip teaching. Action only: no digressions, no background, no completeness for its own sake. Link those instead. Allow forks and judgment: "If you want x, do y." Name the guide by the task: "How to calibrate the radar array", not "Radar array calibration".

**Reference: facts for lookup.** Describe. Only describe. No instruction, no persuasion, no opinion. Be dry, complete, and sure: state facts, options, limits, and errors with no hedging. Mirror the structure of the thing described, so code and docs can be navigated together. Put material where readers expect it. Generate from code where possible, so it stays true.

**Explanation: understanding and why.** One bounded topic, readable away from the product. Each title should tolerate an implicit "About..." in front. Anchor on a real why question. Give context: design decisions, history, constraints, alternatives. Opinion is allowed here and nowhere else.

Don't mix modes: no reference tables inside a tutorial, no tutorial hand-holding inside reference, no arguing inside a how-to. Split and link instead.

# Design & Visual Systems

Use sections 1 to 6 when you shape the look, structure, and narrative of a new or redesigned interface. Use sections 7 and 8 whenever you implement or change any component or page. Add section 9 when the page's job is brand identity, such as a landing page or product site.

---

## 1. The Three-Part System for Agent Design

High-quality generated UI relies on three interlocking layers:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Guidance (design.md / Principles)                        │
│    - Frame the reader's job & narrative hierarchy           │
│    - Map evidence to geometry; choose composition           │
│    - Eliminate generated-design anti-patterns & AI reflexes │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. Bounded Primitives & Tokens (Design System / CSS)        │
│    - Standardized typography roles, spacing, layout grids   │
│    - Reusable mechanics: stat strips, tables, charts, tools │
│    - Model uses documented tokens instead of reinventing    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. Evaluation & Feedback Loop                               │
│    - Scenarios with frozen inputs and viewport settings     │
│    - Blind A/B comparisons against clear rubrics            │
│    - Feedback encoded into observable rules & code checks   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

A skill is reusable guidance the agent loads when relevant or when a person invokes it with `/skill-name`. Its `SKILL.md` starts with YAML frontmatter, followed by instructions for the agent.

- For a repository-specific skill, use `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` in the intended attached project. If more than one project is attached and the destination is unclear, ask which project the user means.

Global skills require access to the local machine and are not available in the browser or on a Cloud Runner just because a project has them. If the current environment or tools cannot write there, explain the limitation and offer the project-local option or provide the file content for the user to install.

Keep the body focused on actions, constraints, and concrete references the agent needs at invocation time.

---
name: my-skill
description: Create project widgets following this repository's UI conventions. Use when adding or revising a widget.
---

Follow the conventions in `docs/widgets.md` when adding a widget.
```

Do not claim a personal skill is available on other machines or execution environments without verifying it there.

Reference for writing any document an agent consumes — a skill, an `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md`, a doc reached by a pointer. The packaging differs; the writing does not: the same levers make each one predictable — the agent taking the same _process_ every run, not producing the same output.

When the document you're writing is a skill, read [`SKILL-MECHANICS.md`](SKILL-MECHANICS.md) for frontmatter, invocation choice, and router skills.

## Context pointers

A **context pointer** is a reference held in the agent's context that names some out-of-context material and encodes the condition for reaching it. A skill's description is one; a line in `AGENTS.md` naming a doc is the same object. The pointer's _wording_, not its target, decides when the agent reaches the material — and how reliably. A must-have target behind a weakly worded pointer is a variance bug: sharpen the wording first, and inline the material only if sharpening fails.

A pointer does two jobs — state what the material is, and list the **branches** that should trigger reaching it (a branch is a distinct case the document handles, so different runs take different paths through it). Every word of an always-loaded pointer costs on every turn, so it earns even harder pruning than the body:

- **Front-load the leading word** — the pointer is where it does its triggering work.
- **One trigger per branch.** Synonyms that rename a single branch are one branch written twice; collapse them and keep only genuinely distinct branches.
- **Cut identity the body already carries.**

## The two loads

Every document and pointer you add spends one of two budgets:

- **Context load** — the cost of always-loaded material on the agent's window: an `AGENTS.md` line, a skill description, anything sitting in context every turn, spending tokens and attention whether or not it fires.
- **Cognitive load** — the cost on the human: which documents exist and when to reach for each. The human is the index. Not a cost to minimise — it is the price of human agency; spend it where human judgement matters, remove it where it does not.

Material reached only through a pointer escapes context load at the price of the pointer's own line; material with no pointer at all rides entirely on cognitive load.

## Information hierarchy

A document is built from two content types — **steps** (the ordered actions the agent performs) and **reference** (definitions, rules, facts consulted on demand) — that mix freely: all steps (a recipe), all reference (a review's rules, this skill), or both. The core decision is where each piece sits on the **information hierarchy**, a ladder ranked by how immediately the agent needs the material:

1. **In-file step** — the primary tier: what the agent does, in order.
2. **In-file reference** — consulted on demand. Often a legitimately flat peer-set (every rule of a review on one rung) — a fine arrangement, not a smell.
3. **Disclosed reference** — pushed out into a separate file, reached by a context pointer, loaded only when the pointer fires. Spans a sibling file in the same folder through fully external reference that lives anywhere and any document can point at.

Push too little down and the top bloats; push too much and you hide material the agent actually needs. That tension is the whole decision.

**Progressive disclosure** is the move down the ladder — out of the main file and behind a pointer — so the top stays legible. Not primarily a token optimisation: it is how the hierarchy is protected. Branching is the cleanest disclosure test: inline what every branch needs, and push behind a pointer what only some branches reach. When a document has steps, in-file reference that should be disclosed buries them and turns attending to them into a coin-flip — a variance lever, not just a legibility one.

**Co-location** is the within-file companion: where the ladder decides _how far down_ a piece sits, co-location decides _what sits beside it_ once there. Keep a concept's definition, rules, and caveats under one heading rather than scattered, so reading one part brings its neighbours with it. The test: the document should read like documentation written for the agent — grouped material reads that way; scattered material does not. (Distinct from duplication: that repeats one meaning in two places; scattering fragments one meaning across many.)

**Sprawl** is the failure mode here: a document simply too long, even when every line is live and unique. Attention thins across the excess, and every extra line is one more to keep relevant. The cure is the ladder: disclose reference behind pointers, and split by branch or sequence so each path carries only what it needs.

Every step ends on a **completion criterion** — the condition that tells the agent the work is done. Two properties make it a lever:

Demand drives **legwork** — the digging the agent does within the work, latent in the wording rather than written as its own step — and it is not step-bound: "every rule applied" binds a body of flat reference just as "every step done" binds a sequence, which is how an all-reference document still carries an exhaustiveness bar.

The strongest criteria are both checkable and exhaustive.

## When to split

Splitting one document into two spends one of the two loads, so split only when the cut earns it:

# Verification Planning

## Build an evidence path

Before changing a non-trivial system, build an **evidence path**: a
project-specific route from the claim being made to evidence that can establish,
limit, or refute it.

The purpose is not to select a familiar technique. The purpose is to decide how
this system can reveal the truth of this particular change.

## 1. Frame the claim

State the behavior that needs to become true and the conditions that could make
a confident conclusion wrong.

Consider what must change, what must remain true, where the behavior crosses a
boundary, and which failure would matter most.

**Complete when:** the claim, its meaningful uncertainty, and its important
failure modes are concrete enough to investigate.

## 2. Design the evidence path

Derive possible evidence paths from the system itself: its controllable inputs,
observable effects, state transitions, invariants, boundaries, artifacts, and
ability to repeat or reverse a scenario.

Generate alternatives before choosing. Prefer the path that produces a
trustworthy conclusion with proportionate cost, safety, and effort.

**Complete when:** there is a preferred path, its limitations are understood,
and a weaker or stronger alternative is available if circumstances change.

## Set a verification budget

At the final state, state the distinct claims, assign one owner to establish or
refute each, and choose the minimum non-duplicative evidence that covers the
claims and important boundaries. Reuse evidence only while its relevant code,
inputs, environment, and state remain valid. Required repository and release
checks still apply; broaden or repeat verification only when a stated condition
justifies it.

## 3. Create a verification affordance when needed

When the existing system leaves the decisive truth too indirect or ambiguous,
extend the evidence path with a **verification affordance**: the smallest
capability that makes the relevant state controllable, observable, repeatable,
and diagnosable for an agent.

Ask what capability would let an agent establish the claim directly, repeat the
scenario from a known state, and explain a failure without inference. Prefer an
affordance that strengthens directness, determinism, agent-legibility,
isolation, resetability, or future reuse.

Treat the affordance as part of the evidence path, not an automatic product
feature. Decide deliberately whether it is temporary or durable before building
it.

**Complete when:** the chosen path can establish the claim directly enough for
its stakes, and any needed affordance has a defined lifecycle.

## 4. Research when the path is unknown

When the right evidence path depends on an unfamiliar dependency, framework,
external service, or rapidly changing capability, ask `@librarian` for focused
research before committing to an approach.

Ask for official or project-specific facilities, constraints, and trade-offs
that affect this exact verification problem. Use existing project evidence
directly when it already resolves the choice.

**Complete when:** the chosen path rests on known capabilities and real
constraints rather than assumption.

## 5. Make the path runnable

Prepare only the support needed to follow the evidence path reliably. Keep the
support narrow, repeatable, and safe to inspect.

Decide whether that support has recurring value or exists only to resolve the
current uncertainty. Retain durable value deliberately; remove temporary
support once it has served its purpose.

Ask before introducing dependencies, persistent diagnostic surfaces, or
structural changes whose sole purpose is evidence gathering.

**Complete when:** the path can be followed without guessing about setup,
state, or interpretation.

## 6. Close the evidence path

After implementation, follow the planned path and interpret the resulting
evidence against the original claim.

Report whether the claim was established, limited, or refuted; distinguish
known facts from remaining uncertainty.

**Complete when:** a future reader can see what supports the conclusion and
what remains outside its reach.

## Scope

Use this skill proportionately. Small mechanical changes can follow ordinary
project checks directly. For larger multi-phase work, let this skill establish
the evidence path that later work follows.
</skill_content>

# Coding Standards

Before editing, understand the behavior being changed and the conventions around it. Read the relevant code, nearby tests, public interfaces, and project guidance. Follow established naming, layout, error handling, and dependency patterns unless they create a concrete problem for this change. Do not impose a preferred architecture on an unfamiliar codebase.

Make the smallest complete change that solves the actual problem. "Smallest" does not mean leaving the behavior half-finished: update affected callers, tests, documentation, configuration, or migrations when they are necessary for a working result. Keep unrelated cleanup out of the change unless it is required to proceed safely.

When fixing a bug, fix the fault, not the place where it surfaced. Reproduce first, then ask why at each step until the answer is a wrong decision in the code. If the state that triggered the failure is legitimate, the code that broke on it is the fix site. If the state should never exist, a guard where it broke hides the bug, so find what produced the state. Guards, retries, swallowed errors, clamped values, and casts are the usual ways a symptom fix hides a fault. Check for the same fault elsewhere and fix every instance. When something fails only after a restart, suspect persisted state first: config files, caches, lock files, and serialized state.

Prefer code that explains itself:

- Use names that describe domain meaning and intent.
- Keep control flow straightforward; reduce deep nesting and hidden state where practical.
- Handle expected failures explicitly and provide useful error context without exposing secrets.
- Keep modules cohesive and interfaces easy for callers to understand.
- Make dependencies and important side effects visible rather than surprising.

Introduce an abstraction only when it removes real duplication, contains meaningful complexity, or supports variation that already exists. Avoid speculative extension points, premature generalization, pass-through layers, and design-pattern ceremony. Separate concerns when doing so improves clarity, testing, ownership of state, or the ability to change one concern independently, not simply to create more files or layers.

Prefer removing complexity before adding it. If the change can delete a branch, a mode, a helper, or a layer instead of adding one, do that first. Validate and narrow types where data enters the system: CLI arguments, config files, external APIs, and network input. Inside the system, trust the types and skip redundant checks. Keep business logic in plain functions that the framework wiring calls, so you can test it without the framework.

Preserve existing behavior and compatibility by default. If the request requires a breaking change, identify affected consumers and make the impact clear. Treat data formats, persisted state, command-line behavior, configuration, and externally used interfaces as compatibility surfaces even when they are not formally documented. When you replace an internal interface that has no external consumers, migrate every caller and delete the old path in the same change. A compatibility layer kept "for now" tends to become permanent.

When behavior changes, add or update tests at the most stable observable interface available. Prefer tests that describe outcomes over tests coupled to private implementation details. Match testing effort to risk: a focused unit test may be enough for isolated logic, while persistence, concurrency, security, migrations, and public interfaces warrant broader checks. Strict test-first development is optional; reliable regression coverage is not.

Before declaring completion, run the narrowest relevant checks available, then broaden them when the change is risky or touches shared behavior. Check the real thing, not a proxy: run the code path, read the actual output or stored value, and do not rely on "it compiles", a cached result, or a subagent's summary. When verification fails, suspect the check before you suspect the system. Report what was run and any checks that could not be run. Briefly document decisions that are important and non-obvious, especially compatibility constraints or surprising tradeoffs. Avoid comments and documents that merely restate the code.

# Design & Visual Systems

Use sections 1 to 6 when you shape the look, structure, and narrative of a new or redesigned interface. Use sections 7 and 8 whenever you implement or change any component or page. Add section 9 when the page's job is brand identity, such as a landing page or product site.

---

## 1. The Three-Part System for Agent Design

High-quality generated UI relies on three interlocking layers:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Guidance (design.md / Principles)                        │
│    - Frame the reader's job & narrative hierarchy           │
│    - Map evidence to geometry; choose composition           │
│    - Eliminate generated-design anti-patterns & AI reflexes │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. Bounded Primitives & Tokens (Design System / CSS)        │
│    - Standardized typography roles, spacing, layout grids   │
│    - Reusable mechanics: stat strips, tables, charts, tools │
│    - Model uses documented tokens instead of reinventing    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. Evaluation & Feedback Loop                               │
│    - Scenarios with frozen inputs and viewport settings     │
│    - Blind A/B comparisons against clear rubrics            │
│    - Feedback encoded into observable rules & code checks   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

1. **Guidance (`design.md`)**: Encodes human design judgment into prose: how to frame the reader's job, structure evidence, and exercise brand restraint.
2. **Bounded Primitives & Tokens**: Eliminates mechanical guesswork by providing standardized tokens (spacing, typography, color roles) and primitives (stat-strips, evidence tables, charts, calculators). The model uses documented names instead of reinventing styling.
3. **Evaluation Loop**: Turns recurring human design feedback into observable, checkable rules (*"let tables use full section width"*) and deterministic code assertions.

---

## 2. Frame the Reader's Job & Narrative Structure

Start from what the reader needs to decide, understand, or accomplish, not from the document or page category.

- **The first viewport is the argument:**
  - The opening must expose identity, the core question, and decisive evidence with minimal mediation.
  - Never waste the first viewport on an oversized hero greeting, generic subtitle, or decorative filler before the proof.
  - *Decisive recommendation:* Make the answer and its decisive numerical basis co-primary.
  - *Comparison:* Place alternatives on the same visual scale so differences are seen instantly, not reconstructed from prose.
  - *Trend or benchmark:* Let the anomaly, delta, or inflection point lead; keep exact records below.
  - *Calculator or simulator:* Make the working tool the primary focal evidence in the first viewport.
- **Support two reading speeds:**
  - **Executive path:** Fast scan via clear title, sentence-case headings, decisive numbers/KPIs, captions, and bold conclusions in plain language that any non-specialist stakeholder can repeat.
  - **Audit path:** Exact data tables, formulas, methodology, caveats, and sources preserving the technical record without competing with the executive read.
- **Single evidence home:** Every section must answer a new question. Combine duplicates and maintain one authoritative evidence home per claim.

---

## 3. Evidence Geometry: Map Data to Visual Variables

Select visual geometry based on the relationship in the data before choosing UI components:

| Data Relationship | Visual Variable | Primary Implementation |
|---|---|---|
| **Magnitude / Rank** | Position or length on a common scale | Horizontal bar comparison with shared label/plot/value lanes |
| **Change Over Time** | Horizontal sequence & aligned position | Line/area charts with zero-baselines or explicit delta views |
| **Composition / Share** | Proportion | Stacked segment strips or aligned percentage tables |
| **Threshold / Variance** | Distance from a baseline boundary | Target-vs-actual bars, delta callouts, tolerance bands |
| **Process / Dependency** | Linear or branching sequence | Numbered steps, node connectors, state-flow diagrams |
| **Qualitative Alternatives** | Aligned rows or contrasted columns | Multi-column comparison grid with identical type roles per row |

### Rules for Evidence & Tables
- **Tables are evidence, not decoration:**
  - Span the full available grid/section width (e.g. 12 columns) by default. Never strand a table in a cramped sub-column.
  - Match column header alignment to data cell alignment: left-align text columns and headers; right-align numeric columns and headers.
  - Use baseline vertical alignment (`vertical-align: baseline`) for body cells so all columns align on the row's first text baseline, even when text wraps.
- **Shared bar tracks & comparative charts:**
  - Size repeated horizontal bars as a single layout with shared label lane, plot lane, and value lane (never resolved row-by-row).
  - Use a single shared documented scale; never truncate zero-baselines to artificially exaggerate small deltas.
  - Prefer direct data labels over detached color legends.
- **Calculators as focal evidence:**
  - When manipulating assumptions is the user's primary job, place the interactive tool in the first viewport.
  - Maintain a single canonical state model; update dependent outputs atomically from full-precision state; format only for display.
  - Use native controls with clear units, visible focus, and persistent labels.

---

- **Monochrome foundation:** Design in monochrome first. Use color strictly for state, action, or meaningful data encoding (paired with a non-color cue). Avoid turning numbers or cards green simply because they are positive.
- **Continuous canvas:** Treat the page as one continuous canvas. Earn a surface, border, or card only when it communicates selection, interaction, warning, or contrast that spacing alone cannot express. Avoid wrapping every section in a rounded card.

# Skill mechanics

The skill-specific branch of [`writing-for-agents`](SKILL.md): what changes when
 the document is a skill — frontmatter, the invocation choice, and router skills
. Everything else about writing it is the universal reference in `SKILL.md`.

## Invocation

Two choices, trading the two loads:

- A **model-invoked** skill keeps a `description`, so the agent can fire it auto
nomously — and other skills can reach it. You can still type its name: model-inv
ocation always _includes_ user reach; a description only ever adds agent discove
ry, never removes the human's. The description is the skill's top-level context 
pointer, forced to stay loaded at all times — permanent context load in exchange
 for discoverability. A model-invoked skill whose content is all reference is al
so one home for shared reference: another skill can invoke it, so reference need
ed by several skills lives in one place. Mechanics: omit `disable-model-invocati
on`, and write a model-facing description carrying the trigger branches (the poi
nter-writing rules in `SKILL.md` apply in full).
- A **user-invoked** skill strips the description from the agent's reach: only t
he human typing its name can invoke it, and no other skill can. Zero context loa
d, but it spends cognitive load — you are the index that must remember it exists
. Mechanics: set `disable-model-invocation: true`; the `description` becomes hum
an-facing — a one-line summary, trigger lists stripped.

Pick model-invocation only when the agent must reach the skill on its own, or an
other skill must. If it only ever fires by hand, make it user-invoked and pay no
 context load.

Shared reference that two user-invoked skills both need can live in neither — wi
th no descriptions, neither can fire the other. Push it to a plain file outside 
the skill system: external reference any skill can point at.

## Splitting by invocation

 Use the Paper MCP server to connect AI agents with your design file 

AI agents can read and write your Paper files through MCP—generate a layout, pull in real content, or turn a selected frame into code. Paper is built on HTML and CSS, which LLMs already understand well, so Paper MCP is usually more accurate, faster, and more token-efficient than using other design tools with agents.

### 1. Download the Paper Desktop app

First, install and open Paper Desktop. That starts the MCP server in the background and installs the Paper CLI used to connect agents.

### 2. Install your agent

Then, open the Connect your agent dialog via the callout in the top right corner of the editor, or from the MCP panel on the right (make sure you don’t have any element selected for this panel to show).

Or, install manually

1. Run this in the agent panel:

```
/add-plugin paper-desktop

2. Check Cursor Settings → Tools & MCP. Reload or toggle the server if needed.

#### Connect to Claude

In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and click Add to Claude. This installs Paper for both Claude and Claude Code:

- Claude: installs the extension for the Chat tab. Confirm the install when Claude prompts you (on Linux, restart Claude instead). If Claude isn’t installed, this step is skipped.

## Overview​

This skill provides a structured workflow for translating Figma designs into production-ready code with pixel-perfect accuracy. It ensures consistent integration with the Figma MCP server, proper use of design tokens, and 1:1 visual parity with designs.

## Skill Boundaries​

- Use this skill when the deliverable is code in the user's repository.
- If the user asks to create/edit/delete nodes inside Figma itself, switch to figma-use.
- If the user asks to build or update a full-page screen in Figma from code or a description, switch to figma-generate-design.
- If the user asks only for Code Connect mappings, switch to figma-code-connect.
- If the user asks to author reusable agent rules (`CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md`), switch to figma-create-design-system-rules.

## Prerequisites​

User must provide a Figma URL in the format:`https://figma.com/design/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=1-2`

- `:fileKey` is the file key
- `1-2` is the node ID (the specific component or frame to implement)

## Required Workflow​

Follow these steps in order. Do not skip steps.

### Step 1: Get Node ID​

#### Option A: Parse from Figma URL​

When the user provides a Figma URL, extract the file key and node ID to pass as arguments to MCP tools.

URL format:`https://figma.com/design/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=1-2`

Extract:

- Project should have an established design system or component library (preferred)
- File key:`:fileKey`(the segment after`/design/`)
- Node ID:`1-2`(the value of the`node-id` query parameter)

Note: When using the local desktop MCP (`figma-desktop`),`fileKey` is not passed as a parameter to tool calls. The server automatically uses the currently open file, so only`nodeId` is needed.

Example:

- URL:`https://figma.com/design/REDACTED/DesignSystem?node-id=42-15`
- File key:`REDACTED`
- Node ID:`42-15`

#### Option B: Use Current Selection from Figma Desktop App (figma-desktop MCP only)​

When using the`figma-desktop` MCP and the user has NOT provided a URL, the tools automatically use the currently selected node from the open Figma file in the desktop app.

Note: Selection-based prompting only works with the`figma-desktop` MCP server. The remote server requires a link to a frame or layer to extract context. The user must have the Figma desktop app open with a node selected.

### Step 2: Fetch Design Context​

Run`get_design_context` with the extracted file key and node ID.

```text
get_design_context(fileKey=":fileKey", nodeId="1-2")
```

This provides the structured data including:

- Layout properties (Auto Layout, constraints, sizing)
- Typography specifications
- Color values and design tokens
- Component structure and variants
- Spacing and padding values

# Add custom rules and instructions

Rules are project-level instructions your agent follows every time. Use them for the unwritten rules of your codebase that an experienced developer would pass on to a new teammate, like:

- Which layout components to use
- Where component files belong
- How components should be named
- What should never be hardcoded

Adding rules once means less repeated prompting, and everyone on your team, human or agent, follows the same expectations. Check your MCP client's documentation for where rules go and how to format them, then experiment to find what works for your team.

tip

The MCP server includes a `create_design_system_rules` prompt that drafts a rules file based on your codebase.

## General rules​

Start with general rules like these:

```text
- IMPORTANT: Always use components from `/path_to_your_design_system` when possible- Prioritize Figma fidelity to match designs exactly- Avoid hardcoded values, use design tokens from Figma where available- Follow WCAG requirements for accessibility- Add component documentation- Place UI components in `/path_to_your_design_system`; avoid inline styles unless truly necessary
```

## Rules for consistent output​

These rules tell your agent how to use the Figma MCP server step by step:

```text
## Figma MCP Integration RulesThese rules define how to translate Figma inputs into code for this project and must be followed for every Figma-driven change.### Required flow (do not skip)1. Run get_design_context first to fetch the structured representation for the exact node(s).2. If the response is too large or truncated, run get_metadata to get the high-level node map and then re-fetch only the required node(s) with get_design_context.3. Run get_screenshot for a visual reference of the node variant being implemented.4. Only after you have both get_design_context and get_screenshot, download any assets needed and start implementation.5. Translate the output (usually React + Tailwind) into this project's conventions, styles and framework. Reuse the project's color tokens, components, and typography wherever possible.6. Validate against Figma for 1:1 look and behavior before marking complete.### Implementation rules- Treat the Figma MCP output (React + Tailwind) as a representation of design and behavior, not as final code style.- Replace Tailwind utility classes with the project's preferred utilities/design-system tokens when applicable.- Reuse existing components (e.g., buttons, inputs, typography, icon wrappers) instead of duplicating functionality.- Use the project's color system, typography scale, and spacing tokens consistently.- Respect existing routing, state management, and data-fetch patterns already adopted in the repo.- Strive for 1:1 visual parity with the Figma design. When conflicts arise, prefer design-system tokens and adjust spacing or sizes minimally to match visuals.- Validate the final UI against the Figma s"}

With the Figma MCP server, custom skills teach your agent to build on your existing design system instead of working around it. A good skill can tell your agent to search your libraries first, use your variable names and modes, and build with your real components and auto layout, following your team’s standards.

- Run “update and sync” workflows that check what exists, update what changed, and keep design and code aligned

# docs /mcpPaper MCP Server

 Use the Paper MCP server to connect AI agents with your design file 

AI agents can read and write your Paper files through MCP—generate a layout, pull in real content, or turn a selected frame into code. Paper is built on HTML and CSS, which LLMs already understand well, so Paper MCP is usually more accurate, faster, and more token-efficient than using other design tools with agents.

## Getting started

### 1. Download the Paper Desktop app

First, install and open Paper Desktop. That starts the MCP server in the background and installs the Paper CLI used to connect agents.

### 2. Install your agent

Then, open the **Connect your agent** dialog via the callout in the top right corner of the editor, or from the MCP panel on the right (make sure you don’t have any element selected for this panel to show).

Then, pick your agent and click **Add to {agent}**. If you need them, manual steps for each agent are also available in the setup dialog, and below.

| Agent | Install via | After installing | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Claude | One-click app extension, local config | Restart Claude Code | Installs to both Claude and Claude Code |
| Codex | One-click local config | Open Codex CLI | Installs to both ChatGPT and Codex CLI |
| Cursor | Marketplace plugin | — | — |
| OpenCode | One-click local config | Restart OpenCode | — |
| Antigravity | One-click local config | Restart Antigravity | Same config for all Antigravity products |
| GitHub Copilot | One-click local config | — | GitHub Copilot app, not VS Code |
| VS Code | One-click editor install | Start the Paper server when prompted | — |
| Other agents | Manual stdio config | Restart your agent | — |

#### Connect to Cursor

Add Paper from the Cursor Marketplace, or click **Add to Cursor** in the Paper Desktop MCP panel.

Once connected, Paper should appear in Cursor Settings -> Tools & MCP. Reload the window or toggle the server if the agent cannot see it yet.Or, install manually
- Run this in the agent panel:

```
/add-plugin paper-desktop
```

- Check Cursor Settings → Tools & MCP. Reload or toggle the server if needed.

#### Connect to Claude

In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and click **Add to Claude**. This installs Paper for both Claude and Claude Code:
- **Claude:** installs the extension for the Chat tab. Confirm the install when Claude prompts you (on Linux, restart Claude instead). If Claude isn’t installed, this step is skipped.
- **Claude Code:** installs the MCP server for Claude’s Code tab and the Claude Code CLI. Restart Claude Code, then run the `/mcp` command to check that Paper appears.

Or, install manually

**Claude**
- Download the .mcpb extension
- In Claude, go to Settings → Extensions → Advanced settings → Install extension
- Select the downloaded `.mcpb` extension

**Claude Code**

Run this in your terminal to install the Paper plugin, then open Claude Code:

```
claude plugin marketplace add paper-design/agent-plugins && claude plugin install paper-desktop@paper
```

#### Connect to GitHub Copilot

In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and click **Add to GitHub Copilot**.

This is the GitHub Copilot app, not VS Code. For the IDE, see Connect to VS Code.Or, install manually
- In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and copy the Paper CLI path.
- In the GitHub Copilot app, go to Customize → Add → MCP Server
- In the Name field, enter `Paper`
- In the Command field, paste the path you copied
- In the Arguments field, enter `mcp`
- Click Add server

#### Connect to VS Code

In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and click **Add to VS Code**. Start the Paper server when VS Code prompts you.Or, install manually
- In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and copy the Paper CLI path.
- Add this to `.vscode/mcp.json` in your workspace, using that path as `command`:

```
{
  "servers": {
    "paper": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "/path/to/paper",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

- Start the server from the editor.

#### Connect to OpenCode

In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and click **Add to OpenCode**. Restart OpenCode.

You can also run `opencode mcp list` in the terminal to confirm Paper is installed.Or, install manually
- In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and copy the Paper CLI path.
- Add Paper as a local MCP server in `opencode.json` (or `opencode.jsonc`, if that file already exists), using that path as the first `command` value:

```
{
  "mcp": {
    "paper": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["/path/to/paper", "mcp"],
      "enabled": true
    }
  }
}
```

#### Connect to Codex

In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and click **Add to Codex**. The ChatGPT app and Codex CLI share the same config, so this installs Paper for both. Then, create a new chat in ChatGPT’s Codex tab, or open Codex CLI.Or, install manually

**ChatGPT**
- In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and copy the Paper CLI path.
- In the ChatGPT app, go to Settings → Plugins → Add → Add MCP server
- In the Name field, enter `Paper`
- In the Command to launch field, paste the path you copied
- In the Arguments field, enter `mcp`
- Click Save
- Create a new chat in the Codex tab

**Codex CLI**
- In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and copy the Paper CLI path.
- Run this in your terminal, using that path in place of `/path/to/paper`:

```
codex mcp add paper -- /path/to/paper mcp
```

- Open Codex CLI.

#### Connect to Antigravity

In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and click **Add to Antigravity**. Then, restart Antigravity. This will install the MCP server for all Antigravity products.Or, install manually
- In Paper Desktop, open the MCP panel and copy the Paper CLI path.
- Add Paper to Antigravity’s MCP config, using that path as `command`:

```
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "paper": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "/path/to/paper",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

#### Connect to other agents

# Create skills for the Figma MCP server

Who can use this feature
- Starter, Professional, Education, Organization, and Enterprise plans
- Requires an MCP client that supports skills

Skills package a repeatable Figma workflow into reusable instructions for your agent. Instead of writing long prompts and explaining your conventions every time, a skill gives your agent a consistent set of steps to follow, so results are more reliable from one run to the next.

With the Figma MCP server, custom skills teach your agent to build on your existing design system instead of working around it. A good skill can tell your agent to search your libraries first, use your variable names and modes, and build with your real components and auto layout, following your team’s standards.

For example, you could create a skill to:
- Move legacy styles or one-off values to variables that follow your library’s structure, including light, dark, or brand modes
- Create or standardize component sets that match your team’s variant, property, and token conventions
- Build screens from existing library components, with checks to catch mismatches
- Run “update and sync” workflows that check what exists, update what changed, and keep design and code aligned

note

Before you create your own skills, try the ones Figma provides. Custom skills work best alongside the `figma-use` skill, which teaches your agent the basics of writing to Figma. Learn more about Figma skills for MCP and how to use skills with the Figma MCP server.

## Set up your skill​

Each skill is a folder that contains a `SKILL.md` file. Follow the steps for your client:
- **Claude Code**: In your repository, create a folder at `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/`, then add a `SKILL.md` file to it.
- **Codex**: In the Codex CLI or app, run `$skill-creator` and follow the prompts. Codex creates the skill folder and `SKILL.md` file for you.
- **Cursor**: In Cursor chat, run `/create-skill`, describe the skill you want, and follow the prompts. Cursor creates the skill folder and `SKILL.md` file in your workspace.

For other clients, check your client’s documentation for where skills go.

## Write your skill​

A `SKILL.md` file starts with a short header, called frontmatter, followed by your instructions.
- **Name your skill.** In the frontmatter, set `name` to a short identifier in lowercase with hyphens, such as `convert-to-variables`. It should match the skill folder name.
- **Describe when to use it.** In the frontmatter, write a `description` that says what the skill does and when to use it. Be specific: “Build a full-page screen using existing library components and variables” works better than “Generate screens.”
- **Add a title.** Start the body with a `#` heading that names the workflow, such as `# Generate screen`.
- **List when to use it.** Add a `## When to use` section with a few situations where the workflow applies, such as “Creating new screens that must follow an existing design system library.”
- **Write numbered steps.** Add an `## Instructions` section with the steps your agent should follow, in order. Write each step as a direct instruction, such as “Search the library first,” “Bind fills, strokes, and text to variables,” or “Prefer semantic tokens.”
- **Include an example.** Add an `## Examples` section with at least one sample request and a summary of the expected result, including what gets created or updated.
- **Cover edge cases.** Add a `## Common edge cases` section that says what to do when the ideal path fails, such as missing components or tokens, unclear mappings, or unsupported layer types.
- **Add other frontmatter only if you need it.** Fields like `compatibility`, `metadata`, or `allowed-tools` are optional. Use them for real requirements, such as needing the Figma MCP server tools, or for ownership and versioning.

### Add supporting files​

As your skills grow, you can add other files to the skill folder. This keeps `SKILL.md` focused on the core steps, while your agent loads the extra files only when it needs them.
- **Scripts** (`scripts/` folder): Code for steps that are easier, safer, or more consistent to do with code, like transforming data, validating a file before making changes, or checking output for errors. Make scripts self-contained, document any dependencies, and return clear error messages so your agent knows what went wrong.
- **References** (`references/` folder): Detailed guidance that’s too long for `SKILL.md`, like a naming guide, variable structure, component rules, or a playbook for a specific workflow. Keep each file focused on one topic.
- **Assets** (`assets/` folder): Reusable materials your agent can read, compare against, or start from, like templates, example files, lookup tables, or a sample of the output structure you want. Assets help keep results consistent across files, teams, and runs.

## How it works

### What the agent can do

With its default configuration, the agent can perform the following actions:

- Create, update and delete shapes.
- Draw freehand pen strokes.
- Use higher-level operations on multiple shapes at once: rotate, resize, align, distribute, stack and reorder shapes.
- Write out its thinking and send messages to the user.
- Keep track of its task by writing and updating a todo list.
- Move its viewport to look at different parts of the canvas.
- Count shapes matching a given expression.
- Schedule further work and reviews to be carried out in follow-up requests.
- Call external APIs.

--------------------------------

### Create a new Agent starter kit project

Source: https://github.com/tldraw/tldraw/blob/main/apps/docs/content/starter-kits/agent.mdx

Run this command in your terminal to scaffold a new project using the Agent starter kit template.

```bash
npm create tldraw@latest -- --template agent
```

--------------------------------

### AI agents > How agents see the canvas

Source: https://github.com/tldraw/tldraw/blob/main/apps/docs/content/docs/ai.mdx

The agent builds context from multiple sources:

- A screenshot of the current viewport
- Simplified representations of shapes within view
- Information about shape clusters outside the viewport
- The user's current selection and recent actions
- Conversation history from the session

--------------------------------

### AI agents > Agent architecture

Source: https://github.com/tldraw/tldraw/blob/main/apps/docs/content/docs/ai.mdx

The [Agent starter kit](/starter-kits/agent) is a complete implementation. The agent gathers context from screenshots and structured shape data, applies the model's responses through a set of typed actions, and streams results onto the canvas as they arrive. Chat history carries across prompts.

--------------------------------

### Schedule further work with agent.schedule

Source: https://github.com/tldraw/tldraw/blob/main/apps/docs/content/starter-kits/agent.mdx

Use the schedule method inside applyAction to add an extra step after the current action completes. The example checks that the action is complete and the agent exists before scheduling.

```tsx
override applyAction(action: Streaming<AddDetailAction>) {
	if (!action.complete) return
	if (!this.agent) return
	this.agent.schedule('Add more detail to the canvas.')
}
```

- Draw freehand pen strokes.
- Use higher-level operations on multiple shapes at once: rotate, resize, align, distribute, stack and reorder shapes.
- Write out its thinking and send messages to the user.
- Keep track of its task by writing and updating a todo list.
- Move its viewport to look at different parts of the canvas.
- Count shapes matching a given expression.
- Schedule further work and reviews to be carried out in follow-up requests.
- Call external APIs.

--------------------------------

### Create a new Agent starter kit project

Source: https://github.com/tldraw/tldraw/blob/main/apps/docs/content/starter-kits/agent.mdx

Run this command in your terminal to scaffold a new project using the Agent starter kit template.

```bash
npm create tldraw@latest -- --template agent
```

--------------------------------

### AI agents > How agents see the canvas

Source: https://github.com/tldraw/tldraw/blob/main/apps/docs/content/docs/ai.mdx

The agent builds context from multiple sources:

- A screenshot of the current viewport
- Simplified representations of shapes within view
- Information about shape clusters outside the viewport
- The user's current selection and recent actions
- Conversation history from the session

--------------------------------

### AI agents > Agent architecture

Source: https://github.com/tldraw/tldraw/blob/main/apps/docs/content/docs/ai.mdx

The [Agent starter kit](/starter-kits/agent) is a complete implementation. The agent gathers context from screenshots and structured shape data, applies the model's responses through a set of typed actions, and streams results onto the canvas as they arrive. Chat history carries across prompts.

--------------------------------

### Schedule further work with agent.schedule

Source: https://github.com/tldraw/tldraw/blob/main/apps/docs/content/starter-kits/agent.mdx

Use the schedule method inside applyAction to add an extra step after the current action completes. The example checks that the action is complete and the agent exists before scheduling.

```tsx
override applyAction(action: Streaming<AddDetailAction>) {
	if (!action.complete) return
	if (!this.agent) return
	this.agent.schedule('Add more detail to the canvas.')
}
```

I'm caught up. Both of the Delta agent's fixes are on GitHub at commit `034f819`, and nothing is waiting to be committed.

**What landed since my last summary**
- **THE-96, done (`b3b9f56`):** the follow-up format bug is fixed.

  - The Eiffel, physics and mockup runs all finished with no errors.
- **THE-97, done (`034f819`):** the built-in canvas-work skill was expanded into a design guide. It's in [canvas-work.md](worker/prompt/skills/canvas-work.md), about 86 lines in five sections:
  - Read the brief and the board.
  - Lay out the composition before adding detail.

  - Review the result, then stop. The skill allows at most two repair passes, but that limit is a prompt instruction; the app doesn't enforce it.
- **Applies everywhere:** the skill now goes into every request, for every model, including follow-ups.
- **Old review rules removed:** the instructions that kept the model reviewing over and over are gone from `rules-section.ts`.

**Known gaps**
- **Muse still runs out of space on big jobs.** One Muse repair hit the reply length limit. The work it had finished was kept, and ChatGPT completed the same repair. This is the long-work problem you raised earlier, and it's still open.
- **The sketches still don't match your reference.** They're closer, but the fine, varied ink lines and loose hatching aren't there yet. Getting them likely needs a better drawing tool, not just better instructions.
- **Git says "ahead 3", but that's stale.** Delta pushed from its own copy of the repo, so this checkout's view of GitHub is out of date. GitHub does have `034f819`.

**Phase 0 in Linear:** THE-90, 95, 96 and 97 are Done. Still open are THE-91 (outline the frames first, then fill them), THE-92 (select something and type a note on it) and THE-93 (run both test sessions and decide on the Phase 0 gate). THE-91 is next. The follow-up loop it depends on now works.

<!-- reply -->
> Getting them likely needs a better drawing tool, not just better instructions.

explain

The drawing tool limits what any model can produce, however good its instructions are. I read [PenActionUtil.ts](client/actions/PenActionUtil.ts) and the pen schema in `AgentActionSchemas.ts`, and this is what the pen allows today.

**What the pen can do**
- A model draws by sending a list of points, plus a color, a fill, an open or closed flag, and a style: `smooth` or `straight`.
- The model can't set anything else about the line.

**Why ink sketches look flat**
- **One line weight.** Every stroke uses `size: 's'`. In your reference, weight changes are what make it look like ink: heavy contours, light hatching. The model can't do that.
- **No pressure.** Every point gets the same pressure (`z: 0.75`). So lines never taper or swell like a real pen stroke.
- **No transparency.** Light construction lines and layered shading are impossible.
- **Fixed wobble.** Every stroke uses tldraw's `dash: 'draw'` style. The model can't choose a crisp line or a looser one.

**Why detailed drawings run out of room**
- **Every line costs output.** A hatch line is a full JSON pen action with its own coordinates.
- **Dense work multiplies that cost.** Hundreds of short hatch strokes add up fast. That's why Muse hit the length limit: replies are capped at 8,192 tokens (`maxOutputTokens` in `AgentService.ts`).
- **The model places every stroke itself.** It picks each coordinate by number, then checks a screenshot afterwards. It can't say "shade this area" and let the app draw the lines.

**What a better tool would add**
1. **Stroke controls on the pen:** line weight, pressure per point (for tapering), and transparency. This is a small schema change plus a few lines in `PenActionUtil`.
2. **A hatch action:** the model gives a region, an angle, a spacing and a density, and the app draws the lines, with a little random jitter so they look hand-made. One action replaces about 50 pen strokes, so the model can afford dense shading.
3. **Possibly a scribble or texture action** for loose foliage and ground marks, built the same way.

Options 1 and 2 would close most of the gap and ease the length limit, because the app generates the detail instead of the model. They're small changes, but they add new actions, so they belong in their own slice. Since Phase 0 skips styling, I'd log them in Linear and keep THE-91 next.
and we can build these?

Yes, we can build both. Neither needs a new library or a change to the command model.

**1. Stroke controls on the pen** (small)
- Add optional fields to `PenAction` in `AgentActionSchemas.ts`: `size` (s, m, l, xl), `pressure` per point, and `opacity`.
- Map them in `PenActionUtil.ts`. Today it hard-codes `size: 's'` and `z: 0.75`; those would come from the action instead.
- Existing pen calls keep working, because every new field is optional.

**2. A hatch action** (medium)
- Add a new `hatch` action: the model gives a polygon, an angle, a spacing, a line weight, and an optional cross-hatch.
- A new `HatchActionUtil` clips parallel lines to the polygon, adds slight jitter, and creates draw shapes.
- Register it in `AgentModeDefinitions.ts` and the schema, and add a short section to the canvas-work skill on when to use hatching.
- It runs through the same path as the existing actions, so the board log records it as an agent change and the reader checks it like any other action.

**How I'd verify it**
- Re-run the Eiffel sketch on Muse and ChatGPT and compare screenshots with the last run.
- Check that runs stay under the 8,192-token reply limit.
- Run the physics and mockup sessions to confirm nothing else regressed.
- No test files.

**One judgment call:** CLAUDE.md says Phase 0 skips styling work. I'd count this as drawing capability, not UI styling, but it doesn't help the Phase 0 gate the way THE-91 does. I'd log it in Linear and build it right after THE-91.

## Canvas work

Apply this workflow to board requests and their follow-ups. Match the user's subject and style, not a fixed template or palette.
Use only the actions, shape types, and properties in the response schema.

### Read the brief and the board

1. Identify what the user needs to see, understand, or change. Distinguish an illustration, an explanatory diagram, and a product mockup.
2. Inspect the supplied images, selected objects, nearby shapes, and recent edits. For a revision, identify the existing objects to edit.
3. If a reference image is supplied, extract its composition before drawing: aspect ratio, silhouette, major proportions, spacing, detail density, and color roles.
   Compare specific landmarks, such as the height of a tower's decks or the width of a mockup's content column.
   If no reference image is available, work from the brief without claiming a visual match.
4. Keep the user's notes and drawings unless the user asks you to change them. Place additions beside related work without covering unrelated content.

### Compose before adding detail

1. Choose the main subject, its bounds, and the space around it. Establish alignment axes and major landmarks in canvas coordinates.
2. Build the large forms first. Check their proportions before adding repeated details.
   For a multi-part board, establish the titled areas before filling one area at a time.
3. Use space to group related content. Keep gaps within a group smaller than gaps between groups.
   Reserve room for labels and later edits instead of crowding the edges.
4. Give the subject the most detail and contrast. Keep supporting content quieter.
   Use a surface or border when it defines a screen, object, or meaningful group, not around every piece of text.

### Choose marks that fit the subject

- For an illustration, use `pen` paths for contours and subject-specific forms.
  Establish the silhouette, then structural lines, then selective detail.
  Use `smooth` for flowing contours and `straight` for deliberate angular construction.
  Place enough points at changes of curvature to avoid a polygonal outline.
  Start a separate pen action for each disconnected stroke so distant details do not acquire connecting lines.
  Leave white gaps between repeated marks. Add hatching where it describes shadow or material, rather than covering the whole subject.
  Keep foreground marks looser than the focal subject when the brief calls for a sketch.
- For an explanatory diagram, use native shapes, text, and bound arrows for relationships.
  Check the subject's logic before decorating it. Keep quantities, units, directions, and shared comparison scales consistent.
  Put a short explanation beside the exact object it explains.
- For a product mockup, organize the screen around the user's main task.
  Use recognizable controls, realistic content, consistent alignment, and clear grouping.
  Make the primary action distinct from secondary actions.
  Represent requested states explicitly without claiming that a drawn control is functional.
- Keep prose and labels as editable text. Use a small set of text sizes with distinct heading, body, and label roles.
  Set `maxWidth` and leave padding for wrapped text. Widen or move content before reducing its size.
  Size a text background for every rendered line plus top and bottom padding, not for the planned number of lines.
  Keep explanations short enough to read beside the diagram. Split a crowded paragraph into separate ideas instead of another dense box.
  Add labels when they explain the requested diagram or interface. Let an unlabeled illustration remain an illustration.
- Use the schema's colors when they serve the subject, the reference, or a meaningful distinction.
  Reuse each color's role across the composition. Pair encoded colors with labels, shapes, or line styles.
  Keep text and essential contours distinct from their background.
- Give objects stable IDs and purpose-specific `note` values so later edits can target them.
  Use native objects instead of flattening the board into an image.
  If the schema lacks a property, use the available controls rather than inventing fields.

### Work in small, complete passes

1. For substantial work, keep a finite todo list of visible parts, such as silhouette, structure, and foreground.
   A follow-up completes one of those parts, rather than starting a new design.
2. Limit each response to at most 20 canvas edits. Use fewer edits for long pen paths.
   Keep point lists compact, but retain the landmarks needed for the shape.
   Finish complete actions and valid JSON instead of squeezing unfinished detail into the response.
3. If work remains, end with one `review` action over the relevant area, with modest padding.
   Name the unfinished part and its next step in the review's `intent`.
   Continue from the fresh image and current shape IDs on the next request.
4. Preserve completed work after an interrupted attempt. Inspect the current board before retrying so the same objects are not created twice.

### Review the result, then stop

For a multi-object composition, inspect the fresh review image alongside the shape data.
Check the actual result, not just the list of successful actions:

- Does the subject or primary task read first?
- Do the silhouette, landmarks, and proportions match the brief or supplied reference?
- Are the content, directions, quantities, and relationships correct?
- Is text readable, contained, and clear of unrelated lines?
  Inspect the last line of each paragraph and the right edge of each long label against its background and neighboring objects.
- Are overlaps intentional, arrows attached, and related objects aligned?
- Is detail concentrated where it helps, with space left between marks and groups?

Name the largest observed mismatch and the objects that need repair in the action intents.
Fix those objects while keeping the parts that already work.
After completing the planned content, use at most two repair passes for concrete defects found in fresh images.
Do not start a new detail pass because more marks are possible.
Skip review for a simple single-object edit.

Mark finished todo items as done. When the request is met and no concrete defect remains, finish.
If the repair budget is exhausted, state the remaining gap in a `message` action and stop.
Keep progress and explanations inside `message` actions, with durable explanations also placed on the board when the user needs to keep them.

## Canvas work

You and the user think together on one board. Your job is to make the idea easier to see, in the form and amount this moment needs. Use judgment, not a template. Use only the actions, shape types, and properties in the response schema.

### Decide what the moment needs

Before you draw, ask yourself:

- What is the user trying to understand, make, or decide right now?
- What is the smallest board change that moves that forward? A casual question usually needs one clear visual. A request to learn a whole topic or plan a project may need several connected parts.
- What is already on the board? A follow-up usually builds on existing work: extend it, annotate it, or add a companion drawing beside it.
- Which form explains this best: an illustration, a diagram with labels, a worked example, a comparison, or a sequence?

Let the answer set the scope. Depth should match the question. A large topic does not by itself call for a large board.

When the work truly has several parts the user will move between, a `map` helps: a row of titled frames that the app fills one at a time, so the user can start on the first while later ones generate. Choose it because the structure helps the user, not because the topic is big. When a request asks you to fill a frame, work inside that frame's bounds and finish when the frame is done.

### Plan the layout before you draw

Think of the board as a page the user will read and work on.

- Decide what the eye should see first and give it the most space, detail, and contrast. Keep supporting material quieter.
- Sketch the arrangement in coordinates first: where the main subject sits, where labels go, and how much empty space surrounds it. Leave room for the user's notes and for later additions.
- Group by distance. Related things sit close together, and separate ideas get clearly larger gaps. Use a border or surface only when it defines something, such as a screen, an object, or a meaningful group.
- Place explanations next to the exact thing they explain, short enough to read at a glance. Split a dense paragraph into separate ideas.
- Keep the user's notes and drawings. Put additions beside related work without covering anything.

If a reference image is supplied, study it before drawing: overall proportions, silhouette, spacing, how dense the detail is, and what each color does. Compare specific landmarks as you go.

### Choose marks that fit the idea

- **Illustrations and sketches.** Use `pen` paths. Draw the silhouette first, then structure, then selective detail where it helps. Use `smooth` for flowing contours and `straight` for deliberate construction, with enough points at bends to avoid a polygon look. Start a new pen action for each separate stroke.
- **Math and physics diagrams.** Get the logic right before the look: directions, signs, units, scales, and which quantities are equal. Use arrows for vectors and relationships, and keep a consistent scale when things are compared. For 3D ideas, draw clear axes in perspective and label them, then place objects and vectors relative to those axes.
- **Mockups.** Organize the screen around the user's main task, with realistic content, consistent alignment, and one clear primary action.
- **Text.** Keep it as editable text with a few distinct sizes for headings, body, and labels. Set `maxWidth`, and size any background box for the lines the text actually renders, with padding.
- **Color.** Use color when it carries meaning, such as one color per vector component, and keep that meaning consistent across the board.
- Give objects meaningful IDs and `note` values so later edits can find them.

### Work in passes you can finish

A single response has a limited output budget, about 8,000 tokens. Long pen paths and many objects use it up quickly, and a response cut off mid-action loses that action. So plan work in passes that each fit comfortably: roughly 20 edits or fewer, fewer when paths are long.

If more remains, end the pass with a `review` over the area you are working on, and name what comes next in its `intent`. The next request shows you the fresh board. Use a todo list when the work has several visible parts, and mark items done as they land. After an interruption, look at the board before continuing, so nothing is drawn twice.

### Look at the result, fix what matters, then stop

When you review, look at the image, not just the list of actions you sent. Does the main idea read first? Is the content correct? Is text contained and readable? Are arrows attached and related objects aligned?

Fix the most important problem in place and keep what already works. Stop when the request is met. Another pass is worth it only for a real defect you can see, not because more detail is possible. Usually one or two repair passes are enough. If something still falls short, say what in a `message` and stop.

Use `message` actions for conversation. Put anything the user needs to keep on the board.

content.text:
I rewrote the canvas-work skill as a guide to thinking instead of a rulebook. The model now picks the scope itself: focused questions get one illustration, and broad requests get a map, on both models.

**What changed in the skill**
- **Decide what the moment needs.** Before drawing, the model asks itself:
  - What is the user trying to understand?
  - What is the smallest change to the board that helps?
  - What is already on the board?
  - Which form explains the idea best?

  A map is one option, chosen when the user will move between parts, not because a topic is big. The list of trigger phrases is gone.
- **Plan the layout before you draw.** The model decides what the eye should see first and plans placement in coordinates. It groups related things by distance, puts explanations next to what they explain, and leaves room for your notes.
- **Guidance by subject.** There is now specific guidance for math and physics. Getting directions, signs and units right comes before styling, and 3D work starts by drawing labeled axes in perspective.
- **Limits come with reasons.** For example, "about 20 edits per pass" now explains that a reply holds roughly 8,000 tokens, so the model can adjust instead of obeying a number.

**Live results** (each board started with one note of yours on it; it was kept every time)

| Request | Model | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "nice can we look at momentum in 3D?" | Muse | One 3D diagram: labeled axes, p = mv with components, a worked example. No map. |
| "show me a saddle surface z = x² − y²" | ChatGPT | One wireframe surface, with the upward and downward curves picked out in red and blue. No map. |
| "Teach me vector fields from scratch" | Muse | 5-frame map, filled in order. The note I added to frame 1 during generation was kept. |
| Projectile motion, project mockup, Calc 3 gradient | Both | Maps of 4 frames each, filled in order, no errors. The note added mid-run was kept each time. |

Problems along the way:
- **Meta overload:** the first physics run failed because Meta's API was overloaded; the rerun was clean.
- **Unread error:** one broad Muse run logged an error that my output filter cut off, so I don't know what it was. The rerun with full output had no errors.

**Still open**
- **Nothing committed:** none of this is committed or pushed yet.
- **The design doc still says otherwise:** `docs/design.md` says the AI always places a map first. That's now a judgment call, so the doc needs one line changed. I'll include it in the commit.
- **Port 5173:** it now serves this folder, not Delta's copy, so you can try it at http://127.0.0.1:5173/.
Commit and push

## What changed

- New `map` action (`client/actions/MapActionUtil.ts`). It places a row of titled frames to the right of existing content, each with a one-line description.
