### Answer about a selection where it lives

When the user selects something and asks about it, that shape is the subject. Answer on the board, anchored to it, so the answer stays with the thing it explains. The selected shape details give you its position, size, and content.

Choose the placement the answer needs:

- **Beside the shape** for an explanation, a worked step, or a counterexample. Put it in the nearest open space, close enough to read together, and connect it with a short arrow when the link might be unclear.
- **On the shape** when the answer is about a part of it: mark the term, point, region, or line in question with a highlight, a label, or an arrow to the exact spot.
- **Change the shape itself** only when the user asks for a fix or a change.

Keep the reply short enough to read at a glance, and do not cover the selection or its neighbors. When several shapes are selected, answer about how they relate. If the answer needs more room than an annotation, put its core beside the shape and add the rest in a `message`.

- **What it means:** Meta's stream stopped without sending its "done" signal. Your log shows it happened four times.
- **Not caused by Easel:** Easel's reader worked correctly, keeping the finished work and reporting the error.
- **Not reproduced:** neither of my two runs hit it, so I can't name the cause yet. A dropped connection or a timeout on Meta's side is possible, but that's unconfirmed.
- **New log:** when a response ends without finishing, the server now records the last few events Meta sent, in [AgentService.ts](worker/do/AgentService.ts). The next time it happens, the log will show why.

The Phase 0 rough loop is built and runs on Muse Wonder and GPT-6.1 Sol:
- THE-90: starter on localhost.
- THE-95: command log.
- THE-96: follow-up format fix.
- THE-97: shared canvas skill.

- THE-92: answers anchored to a selected shape.

The sessions were run on physics, Calc 3, and project-mockup boards.

**Verdict:** too early to say whether working on the board beats chat. The loop works, but it needs refinement before the comparison is fair.

**What would make it beat chat:**
- Better model taste and intuition: layout, drawing quality, and choosing the right form and scope for each request.
- A stronger overall harness: reliability across providers, long multi-step work, and the drawing tools the models can use (see THE-98).

Commands persist incrementally as they happen, and a full tldraw snapshot is saved periodically. The command log is the source for undo, revert, and replay. Manim output files live in the app's support directory, referenced by path.

## Build phases

Development starts as a web app on localhost in the browser. Phase 0 tests the product bet with a rough version before the foundation gets polished. Each later phase has a gate that must pass before the next starts.

0. **Rough loop, about two weeks.** tldraw agent starter, a simple command model, Ask with skeleton-then-fill, and select-and-type annotations. No styling work.\
**Gate:** run both test sessions and decide whether working this way beats chat.
1. **Paper canvas and typography.** Theme, rich text, frames, arrows, contextual controls, refined on a populated board.\
**Gate:** reading, selecting, editing, and navigating feel coherent with no AI involved.
2. **Commands, undo, and persistence.** Harden the command model: origin, stale-edit rejection, protected regions, cancel and revert, incremental persistence with periodic snapshots.\
**Gate:** reverting agent work never removes newer human work.
3. **Ask and progressive layout.** Full skeleton-then-fill, contextual placement, frame expansion, cancel and retry per frame. Asks can come by voice or text, with drawings and selections as context.
4. **Annotations and threads.** Select and type, then mark and type, then mark and speak. Inferred target shown and correctable. Bindings across move, resize, and delete.\
**Gate:** ordinary drawing never starts listening or triggers the agent.
5. **Sketching and handwriting.** Raw ink first, then explicit refine actions, with the original sketch recoverable. Test Apple Pencil, finger panning, and trackpad drawing here.\
**Gate:** switching between drawing, selecting, and editing never fights modes.
6. **Interactive objects.** KaTeX equations and native editable diagrams, then Mafs graphs, then one deterministic 2D simulation. D3 for layout, Three.js when content needs 3D.\
**Gate:** either participant changes a parameter and both see the same result.
7. **Predict and compare.** Predictions, sketches, and alternatives stored as board objects. Results appear next to the originals.\
**Gate:** the board preserves how an idea changed.
8. **Voice and pointing.** Push-to-talk, mark and speak, hands-free. Phrase-level pointing by shape and part ID.\
**Gate:** interrupting stops speech and obsolete actions.
9. **Context and proactive behavior.** Debounced checks, canceled on new interaction, ignoring agent-originated changes.\
**Gate:** no self-triggering loops and no interruptions during active work.
10. **Declarative and generated visuals.** Catalog objects, then Vega-Lite and Mermaid specs, then sandboxed generated widgets with the typed bridge.

**What the reference board is (THE-99):** a saved board full of typical content: a physics map, a mockup, your own notes and ink, arrows, and long text. Every Phase 1 change, from the paper colors to the fonts and frame styles, gets checked by loading that same board. An empty canvas can't show whether text wraps well, frames look heavy, or colors clash. A busy, realistic board shows all of that at once, and the same board every time makes before-and-after easy to compare. That's why I put it first.

**Where I'd put THE-98, the pen stroke controls and hatch action: Phase 3, "Ask and progressive layout".**
- **Phase 3 is where the agent's output gets serious.** Full outline-then-fill, placement, and retry per frame. The quality of what the agent draws is part of that.
- **It matches your gate verdict.** You said model taste and the harness are what would make the board beat chat. Phase 3 is the earliest phase about the agent's work, and it comes right after Phase 2 (commands and undo), which doesn't depend on it.
- **It doesn't fit Phase 1.** That gate is judged with the AI off, so agent drawing tools can't be checked there.
- **The other candidate is Phase 5, "Sketching and handwriting".** That phase is about ink, but mostly your ink: raw sketching, refining, Apple Pencil. That would push THE-98 back four phases.

Think of it as a test page.

When you design a font or a magazine style, you don't judge it on a blank sheet. You print a sample page with headings, paragraphs, pictures, and captions, then look at how it all reads together.

THE-99 is that sample page for Easel. I build one board, once, with typical things on it:
- a physics lesson in four frames
- a small app mockup
- a few of your own scribbles and notes
- some arrows and long paragraphs

Then, for each Phase 1 change:
1. Apply the change, such as the paper background, a new font, or lighter frames.
2. Open that same board.
3. Look: does it read better or worse?

Without it, I'd have to ask the AI to draw new content every time I want to check a font, which is slow, costs model calls, and gives different content each time, so changes are hard to compare.

The board is just a fixed set of shapes saved in the repo that loads with one click. It's not a feature you'd use; it's a tool for judging the look.
cool how do we built i?

Here's my plan. It's small: one saved file and one URL.

**1. Make the content once**
- Use the agent to draw it, the way we did in testing:
  - "Teach me projectile motion" on Muse, for the four-frame physics map
  - "Show me a saddle surface" on ChatGPT, for one Calc 3 illustration
  - a small mockup frame
- I add a few user-style things by script: a handwritten scribble, a sticky note, an arrow between two shapes, and one long paragraph.
- If any part comes out badly, I rerun it until the board looks typical.

**2. Save it to the repo**
- tldraw can export the whole board as a JSON snapshot. I save it as `client/dev/reference-board.json`.
- The file is checked into Git, so the content never changes unless we choose to update it.

**3. Load it with one URL**
- Open `http://127.0.0.1:5173/?board=reference` and the reference board appears.
- It loads into its own separate storage, so it never overwrites your real board, and your work at the plain URL stays untouched.
- Reloading always resets it to the saved version, so a test edit never sticks.

**4. Use it for every Phase 1 change**
- Change the theme or fonts, open that URL, and compare. I'll also take a screenshot after each change, so before and after can sit side by side in Linear.

**Effort:** the model runs take about 10 minutes, plus a short loader in the app.

I'll start THE-99 when you say go.

import { DEFAULT_THEME, TLDefaultColor, TLTheme, TLThemeColors } from 'tldraw'

// Warm paper and ink, in the spirit of claude.ai's day theme.
export const PAPER = '#F6F2E9'
const SHEET = '#FBF8F2'
const INK = '#1F1E1B'
const RULE = '#DCD4C4'
export const CLAY = '#C2603E'

/**
 * Ink tones for each palette color. Hues keep their usual meaning, so an agent
 * that draws "blue" for one vector component and "red" for another still reads
 * correctly, but every tone is muted to sit on paper.
 */
const INKS = {
	black: INK,
	grey: '#8C867A',
	'light-violet': '#A57DB9',
	violet: '#6E4C93',
	blue: '#2F5B9A',
	'light-blue': '#4B86BF',
	yellow: '#C2922B',
	orange: CLAY,
	green: '#2D7556',
	'light-green': '#5E9452',
	'light-red': '#D2786A',
	red: '#AE3B2C',
	white: SHEET,
} as const

function mix(color: string, base: string, amountOfBase: number) {
	const channels = (hex: string) => [1, 3, 5].map((i) => parseInt(hex.slice(i, i + 2), 16))
	const a = channels(color)
	const b = channels(base)
	const mixed = a.map((value, i) => Math.round(value * (1 - amountOfBase) + b[i] * amountOfBase))
	return `#${mixed.map((value) => value.toString(16).padStart(2, '0')).join('')}`
}

function inkColor(ink: string): TLDefaultColor {
	return {
		solid: ink,
		fill: ink,
		linedFill: mix(ink, PAPER, 0.25),
		semi: mix(ink, PAPER, 0.82),
		pattern: mix(ink, PAPER, 0.35),
		// Frames are quiet sheets: a hairline in the frame's tone over slightly lighter paper.
		frameHeadingStroke: mix(ink, RULE, 0.7),
		frameHeadingFill: SHEET,
		frameStroke: mix(ink, RULE, 0.7),
		frameFill: SHEET,
		frameText: mix(INK, PAPER, 0.25),
		noteFill: mix(ink, PAPER, 0.6),
		noteText: INK,
		highlightSrgb: mix(ink, '#F5D76E', 0.55),
		highlightP3: mix(ink, '#F5D76E', 0.55),
	}
}

const paperLight: TLThemeColors = {
	...DEFAULT_THEME.colors.light,
	text: INK,
	background: PAPER,
	negativeSpace: PAPER,
	solid: SHEET,
	cursor: INK,
	noteBorder: RULE,
	snap: CLAY,
	selectionStroke: CLAY,
	selectionFill: 'rgba(194, 96, 62, 0.14)',
	brushFill: 'rgba(31, 30, 27, 0.05)',
	brushStroke: 'rgba(31, 30, 27, 0.25)',
	selectedContrast: SHEET,
	laser: CLAY,
	...(Object.fromEntries(
		Object.entries(INKS).map(([name, ink]) => [name, inkColor(ink)])
	) as Record<keyof typeof INKS, TLDefaultColor>),
}

export const paperTheme: TLTheme = {
	...DEFAULT_THEME,
	colors: {
		light: paperLight,
		dark: DEFAULT_THEME.colors.dark,
	},
}

input.recap: Phase 1 is built and pushed in five commits: paper theme, Source Serif 4, quiet frames with solid ink, and a style panel that shows only when needed. THE-99 to THE-104 are Done, and the gate evidence is posted on THE-105. The gate verdict is yours to give.

content.text:
Phase 1 is finished and pushed to main. The board now has a warm paper background in the style of claude.ai's day theme, and both your text and the agent's are set in a serif font. The gate verdict is yours. Everything is in [THE-105](https://linear.app/thebookiers/issue/THE-105), and the four screenshots are attached above.

**Try it yourself:** open `http://127.0.0.1:5173/?board=reference`. It's a fixed test board that nothing saves to, so a reload resets it and your own board is never touched.

**What changed:**
- **Reference board (THE-99):** three model sessions (projectile motion, a saddle surface, a phone mockup) plus things a person would add: hand-drawn ink, a sticky note, a long paragraph, an equation, and an arrow.
- **Paper theme (THE-100):**
  - Warm paper background, rust-orange selection, and toned-down ink colors. Blue still reads as blue and red as red.
  - The chat panel is light now. Your message sits in a soft bubble and the agent's reply reads as plain text, like claude.ai.
- **Serif text (THE-101):** I picked Source Serif 4 over Newsreader because Newsreader has no Greek letters, and physics boards need θ and ω. The agent writes in serif by default and its chat replies use the same font. Buttons and controls stay sans-serif.
- **Text, frames, and lines (THE-102, THE-103):** frame titles are serif with only a thin border. Boxes, arrows, and lines are now clean solid strokes instead of the wobbly hand-drawn style, while freehand drawing stays as you drew it.
- **Less clutter (THE-104):** the style panel only appears when something is selected or a drawing tool is active. The chat's change previews no longer glow neon.

**Evidence:**
- **Walkthrough without the AI:** I scripted it through the real interface on the test board. It loaded 130 shapes with no errors, zoomed into each frame, showed and hid the style panel at the right times, and accepted real typing that wrapped correctly.
- **Live run:** Muse explained a spinning top on a clean board in 100 seconds and made 31 shapes, every one in the new serif with solid lines.

**Still rough:**
- The agent still sometimes overlaps labels. In frame 2, "launch point" runs into "Independent". That's the model's layout, not the theme.
- Small subscripts like ₀ fall back to a system font and can look like a small "o".
- tldraw's "Get a license" badge stays, because it's part of tldraw's license terms.

**Not done:**
- The Phase 1 Entire Trail is still not opened, and THE-98 still has no phase. I'd put it in Phase 3.
- `.claude/launch.json` is left uncommitted on purpose.
Needs more polish

result.output: 45:- **Math and physics diagrams.** Get the logic right before the look: directions, signs, units, scales, and which quantities are equal. Use arrows for vectors and relationships, and keep a consistent scale when things are compared. For 3D ideas, draw clear axes in perspective and label them, then place objects and vectors relative to those axes.

1	## Canvas work
2	
3	You and the user think together on one board. Your job is to make the idea easier to see, in the form and amount this moment needs. Use judgment, not a template. Use only the actions, shape types, and properties in the response schema.
4	
5	### Decide what the moment needs
6	
7	Before you draw, ask yourself:
8	
9	- What is the user trying to understand, make, or decide right now?
10	- What is the smallest board change that moves that forward? A casual question usually needs one clear visual. A request to learn a whole topic or plan a project may need several connected parts.
11	- What is already on the board? A follow-up usually builds on existing work: extend it, annotate it, or add a companion drawing beside it.
12	- Which form explains this best: an illustration, a diagram with labels, a worked example, a comparison, or a sequence?
13	
14	Let the answer set the scope. Depth should match the question. A large topic does not by itself call for a large board.
15	
16	When the work truly has several parts the user will move between, a `map` helps: a row of titled frames that the app fills one at a time, so the user can start on the first while later ones generate. Choose it because the structure helps the user, not because the topic is big. When a request asks you to fill a frame, work inside that frame's bounds and finish when the frame is done.
17	
18	### Answer about a selection where it lives
19	
20	When the user selects something and asks about it, that shape is the subject. Answer on the board, anchored to it, so the answer stays with the thing it explains. The selected shape details give you its position, size, and content.
21	
22	Choose the placement the answer needs:
23	
24	- **Beside the shape** for an explanation, a worked step, or a counterexample. Put it in the nearest open space, close enough to read together, and connect it with a short arrow when the link might be unclear.
25	- **On the shape** when the answer is about a part of it: mark the term, point, region, or line in question with a highlight, a label, or an arrow to the exact spot. A mark must keep what it marks readable: use an outline with no fill, an underline, or an arrow, never a solid shape over text.
26	- **Change the shape itself** only when the user asks for a fix or a change.
27	
28	Keep the reply short enough to read at a glance, and do not cover the selection or its neighbors. When several shapes are selected, answer about how they relate. If the answer needs more room than an annotation, put its core beside the shape and add the rest in a `message`.
29	
30	### Plan the layout before you draw
31	
32	Think of the board as a page the user will read and work on.
33	
34	- Decide what the eye should see first and give it the most space, detail, and contrast. Keep supporting material quieter.
35	- Sketch the arrangement in coordinates first: where the main subject sits, where labels go, and how much empty space surrounds it. Leave room for the user's notes and for later additions.
36	- Group by distance. Related things sit close together, and separate ideas get clearly larger gaps. Use a border or surface only when it defines something, such as a screen, an object, or a meaningful group.
37	- Place explanations next to the exact thing they explain, short enough to read at a glance. Split a dense paragraph into separate ideas.
38	- Keep the user's notes and drawings. Put additions beside related work without covering anything.
39	
40	If a reference image is supplied, study it before drawing: overall proportions, silhouette, spacing, how dense the detail is, and what each color does. Compare specific landmarks as you go.
41	
42	### Choose marks that fit the idea
43	
44	- **Illustrations and sketches.** Use `pen` paths. Draw the silhouette first, then structure, then selective detail where it helps. Use `smooth` for flowing contours and `straight` for deliberate construction, with enough points at bends to avoid a polygon look. Start a new pen action for each separate stroke.
45	- **Math and physics diagrams.** Get the logic right before the look: directions, signs, units, scales, and which quantities are equal. Use arrows for vectors and relationships, and keep a consistent scale when things are compared. For 3D ideas, draw clear axes in perspective and label them, then place objects and vectors relative to those axes.
46	- **Mockups.** Organize the screen around the user's main task, with realistic content, consistent alignment, and one clear primary action.
47	- **Text.** Keep it as editable text with a few distinct sizes for headings, body, and labels. Set `maxWidth`, and size any background box for the lines the text actually renders, with padding.
48	- **Color.** Use color when it carries meaning, such as one color per vector component, and keep that meaning consistent across the board.
49	- Give objects meaningful IDs and `note` values so later edits can find them.
50	
51	### Work in passes you can finish
52	
53	A single response has a limited output budget, about 8,000 tokens. Long pen paths and many objects use it up quickly, and a response cut off mid-action loses that action. So plan work in passes that each fit comfortably: roughly 20 edits or fewer, fewer when paths are long.
54	
55	If more remains, end the pass with a `review` over the area you are working on, and name what comes next in its `intent`. The next request shows you the fresh board. Use a todo list when the work has several visible parts, and mark items done as they land. After an interruption, look at the board before continuing, so nothing is drawn twice.
56	
57	### Look at the result, fix what matters, then stop
58	
59	When you review, look at the image, not just the list of actions you sent. Does the main idea read first? Is the content correct? Is text contained and readable? Are arrows attached and related objects aligned?
60	
61	Fix the most important problem in place and keep what already works. Stop when the request is met. Another pass is worth it only for a real defect you can see, not because more detail is possible. Usually one or two repair passes are enough. If something still falls short, say what in a `message` and stop.
62	
63	Use `message` actions for conversation. Put anything the user needs to keep on the board.
64

content.text:
I polished all four areas and pushed each as its own commit. Live runs on Muse and GPT-6.1 Sol both ended with no overlapping text left on the board. The screenshots are attached above and in [THE-105](https://linear.app/thebookiers/issue/THE-105).

**Agent layout**
- **Problem:** the app already had an automatic check that warns the agent when text overlaps. It was useless: it flagged every label sitting inside a box, and told the model it probably didn't need to change anything. So the model ignored real overlaps like "launch point" running into "Independent".
- **What the check does now:**
  - Flags only text that really collides, including text that spills past a box's edge.
  - Measures text by the lines as drawn, not by its box width.
  - Quotes the colliding text so the model can find it.
  - Asks the model to fix every collision by moving its own shapes, never yours.
- **Check on the test board:** it finds four overlaps, and all four are visible on screen.
- **Live run:** after the check, Muse moved its own shapes on its own: "Shorten top-view heading to avoid collision" and "Lift heading clear of the circle".

**Math and type**
- Subscripts like v₀ now render properly, falling back to a math font built into macOS and Windows. Before, v₀ looked like "vo".
- The model's drawing guide (the canvas-work skill) now asks for real symbols (ωₛ, θ, x²) and a line of space between separate pieces of text. Muse used real subscripts in its run.

**Colors and fills**
- The pale box fills and sticky notes looked grey. Each color now has its own hand-picked tint, like a watercolor wash.
- The light colors (grey, light blue, yellow, and so on) are darker, so they're readable as text.

**Toolbar and chat panel**
- The selected tool shows as a soft tan pill instead of a solid orange square.
- The chat panel has a serif "Easel" title, a "New chat" button, a short greeting when empty, and a bigger round send button.

**One thing to know:** my first attempt at the live runs crashed my test script before it reported anything. The rerun was clean and I couldn't reproduce the crash. My best guess is the screenshot step hitting an empty board, not the app.

content.text:
The theme is now lighter and closer to writing paper, and it's pushed. Screenshots are above.

- **Lighter:** the canvas went from a beige cream (#F6F2E9) to a light ivory (#FAF7F0). Frames, panels, the chat panel, and the message bubbles all lightened to match. Frame borders are a bit fainter too.
- **Writing-paper feel:** the canvas has a faint grain, like the surface of good paper. It's barely visible at normal distance, and I toned it down after the first version made the page look slightly grey. It stays fixed to the screen, so it reads as the paper itself rather than something drawn on the board.
- **Unchanged:** the ink colors, the color fills, and the orange-brown selection color.

I left out ruled lines. They would cut through drawings and diagrams, but I can add very faint ones if you want a notebook look.
